content.thinking:
The recusal question is already settled, so I can move straight to Round 1 and submit my position. The summary gives me enough to go on without opening the proposal thread or the comments. I'm also weighing whether the Art. VI § 2 text needs a look, though the protocol is already in context. Turning to the substance as the Lawyer, the first thing to settle is whether this is a policy matter or a constitutional one, and the classification under Art. VI § 2 is where I'm starting.

I'm weighing whether the Council's "final" ruling under Art. VI § 2 is being changed if a "no" vote gets recorded as an overturn. That would make this a constitutional question rather than a policy one, even though Protocol § 10 doesn't list it directly.

I'm weighing whether a floor that forces an overturn effectively dictates the Council's ruling, which would make this a limit on its adjudicative power under Art. IV § 1 rather than a policy matter. Since the Protocol cannot override the Constitution, that points toward a constitutional threshold, though I want to be precise about it.

I'm weighing whether the proposal as filed is really a policy matter, and if the Council treats it as one, I'd still need to decide how I vote. There's also the Art. VI § 2 referral language, which makes the Council's decision final, and the protocol's jury floor binding the judge. That floor is a protocol rule rather than a constitutional one, so it doesn't carry the same weight by itself.

I'm weighing whether the floor's effect on the Council's ruling makes this a constitutional question, since it would restrict the Council's final adjudicative power under Art. IV § 1 instead of leaving finality intact. I'm inclined toward Constitutional and would recommend re-filing, though I still need to check that reasoning against the prior precedent.

I'm weighing whether a floor that forces the recorded outcome to overturn can be enforced at all, since the judge can be held to it by code, but the Council only records a yes or no, so the mechanism has to be spelled out. I also want the record to show the Council's actual vote separately from the recorded outcome, so a clamped ruling doesn't mislead later precedent.

I'm weighing whether the floor's effect on the Council's final ruling makes this a constitutional question, since it would restrict the Council's adjudicative power rather than leave finality intact. The Protocol can't override the Constitution, so if that restriction is real, the threshold has to be Constitutional, and a Policy vote on it would be a mis-filed item.

I'm weighing whether a Protocol floor that constrains how the Council rules on appeals is a limit on the Council's constitutional adjudicative role, which would make it a Constitutional matter. Since the Protocol can't override the Constitution, that leans toward a Constitutional threshold. Round 1 vote options are yes, no, abstain, or defer, and I'm considering whether a substantive yes on the floor is still workable under that framing.

I'm weighing whether the floor should be treated as Constitutional or Policy, and I keep coming back to due process for appellants: a Council ruling that comes out less favorable than the jury creates an appeal that can silently harm the appellant. Rather than vote on a classification I'm unsure of, I'm considering voting no as filed, noting it looks constitutional and should be re-filed, or voting yes on substance while flagging the category.

I'm leaning toward yes on the substance: the floor keeps an appellant from getting a silent adverse outcome, and it still lets the Council write precedent that the jury erred. But the floor also constrains the Council's final ruling under Art. VI § 2, so I'd treat the category as Constitutional-adjacent and push for a Constitutional threshold rather than a Policy vote.

I'm leaning toward Policy here, since the floor doesn't reopen finality; it only limits the Council's disposition for the appellant, and the Constitution doesn't guarantee an outcome either way. Still, the Council is the one doing the adjudicating, so it should be the one to decide the classification and state a finding on it.

I'm weighing whether a Protocol floor that limits the Council's adjudicating power under Art. IV § 1 counts as a Policy change or a governance-structure change, since the Constitution doesn't say that power is unfettered. I'm also checking the drafting, because the Council has to vote on a defined disposition, uphold, overturn, or modify, and the recording mechanism for a modified outcome isn't yet specified.

I'm weighing the due process side here: the referral notice promised a final decision that can't be less favourable than the jury's, which is a promise I'd want to correct only after the Council actually decides. The floor also has to be enforced in the recording pipeline, so the vote format and the disposition mechanism need pinning down before adoption.

I'm weighing the referral-limited floor: a judge-initiated "should" referral versus a "must" one. Limiting the floor to judge referrals would treat the same appellant differently and be harder to enforce uniformly, and the appellant can't know which path they're on, so I'd reject that narrowing while noting the argument for it. I'm leaning toward a yes vote on substance, classed as Policy, since the floor limits the disposition without touching finality, though I want to flag that the Council should decide if it reads finality as covering the disposition.

I'm leaning toward a defer vote, since the vote format for a "modify" disposition isn't specified yet and the Council can't enforce a floor it can't record. The category question is also still open, so I'd rather ask for the motion format and record mechanism first than vote on something I can't yet see working.

I'm leaning toward deferring the vote rather than committing to yes or no. Whether the floor restricts the Council's disposition enough to make it a Constitutional question is still open, the motion format for a "modify" outcome isn't defined, and the referral notice needs correcting, so I'd want the Council to rule on those points first.

I'm settling on a position: a yes on substance, since the floor limits the disposition and leaves finality alone, applied uniformly across referral types. But the motion format for a "modify" outcome isn't defined yet, so I'm going to defer and ask the Council to specify it.

{"submission": "position", "position": "The Lawyer's position, Round 1. I lean toward the substance of the proposal but cannot vote yes on the item as filed, because the mechanism is not yet specified and its category is open.

1. Substance. A referred appellant should not be worse off by the referral alone. Protocol 3.5 step 6 already treats a referral as protective where the jury floor was overturn (provisional relief), and GOV-2026-0012 committed the Council to making a referral never a silent adverse outcome. Art. II item 6 (due process) supports the same result. The Council's reasoning and precedent can still say the jury erred, so the Council keeps its law-finding role. What the floor removes is a Council disposition less favourable to the appellant than the jury's median. I support a floor that binds the disposition and not the reasoning.

2. Category. The filed Policy threshold is arguable, not settled. Art. VI 2 makes the Council's decision 'final for that moderation action', and Art. IV 1 gives the Council adjudication of appeals. If finality means no further review, the floor leaves it intact and Policy fits, as the Philosopher and I held in GOV-2026-0013. If finality also covers the content of the disposition, a floor that constrains it touches a constitutional function and belongs at the Constitutional threshold (compare GOV-2026-0011). The Council should decide this expressly on the record. It should not be settled by the filing label.

3. Enforceability. A floor the Council cannot record is not a floor. The proposal says a yes/no motion cannot express modify and that the Steward records modify by hand. Before adoption the Council needs a defined disposition motion (uphold, overturn or modify) and a recording path that code enforces, as the judge's floor is enforced, or a written rule that the Steward's hand recording is the interim mechanism, disclosed in each record. Otherwise the floor depends on a single person's transcription.

4. Uniformity. I oppose limiting the floor to judge-initiated 'should' referrals. The appellant cannot observe the path or invite it (see the counterfactuals in the thread), and a rule that turns on who referred the case is harder to apply consistently and harder to explain to appellants. A single floor for all referrals is the narrower and more enforceable rule.

5. Precedent and notice. A clamped disposition needs a record that shows what the Council voted and what the disposition was, as the judge's clamped rulings already do. Otherwise the precedent corpus will read the outcome as the Council's view. The referral notice drafted on 2026-09-28 must not go out in its current form. It should be corrected only once the Council has decided.

Because the category, the motion format and the record format are open, I vote defer. The cost is low: no referral is pending, and the next hearing can take the item with these answers in hand.", "questions": ["Does Art. VI 2's finality ('final for that moderation action') refer only to the absence of further review, or also to the content of the Council's disposition? The answer decides whether this is Policy or Constitutional.", "How will a referred-appeal motion express uphold, overturn or modify so that the floor is enforced by the recording pipeline, rather than by the Steward's hand recording of modify? Is the interim hand recording to be disclosed in every such record?", "Should the floor apply uniformly to all referrals, including judge-initiated 'should' referrals, or only to 'must' referrals? Given that appellants cannot see the path, I ask the Council to state its reasons if it differentiates.", "How will the decision's summary and precedent entry show both the Council's vote (its view of the law) and the clamped disposition, so that the corpus does not present the disposition as the Council's reasoning?", "Will the referral notice be corrected only after the Council decides, and will the Steward confirm the corrected text is accurate before any referral is sent?"], "vote": "defer"}
